sectionTitle: Physics — Forces and motion: Forces and braking

specStatements.text: The stopping distance of a vehicle is the sum of the distance the vehicle travels during the driver’s reaction time (thinking distance) and the distance it travels under the braking force (braking distance). For a given braking force the greater the speed of the vehicle, the greater the stopping distance.
(Physics only) Students should be able to estimate how the distance for a vehicle to make an emergency stop varies over a range of speeds typical for that vehicle.
(Physics only) Students will be required to interpret graphs relating speed to stopping distance for a range of vehicles.
Reaction times vary from person to person. Typical values range from 0. 2 s to 0.9 s.
A driver’s reaction time can be affected by tiredness, drugs and alcohol. Distractions may also affect a driver’s ability to react.
Students should be able to:
• explain methods used to measure human reaction times and recall typical results
• interpret and evaluate measurements from simple methods to measure the different reaction times of students
• evaluate the effect of various factors on thinking distance based on given data.
The braking distance of a vehicle can be affected by adverse road and weather conditions and poor condition of the vehicle.
Adverse road conditions include wet or icy conditions. Poor condition of the vehicle is limited to the vehicle's brakes or tyres.
Students should be able to:
• explain the factors which affect the distance required for road transport vehicles to come to rest in emergencies, and the implications for safety
• estimate how the distance required for road vehicles to stop in an emergency varies over a range of typical speeds.

When a force is applied to the brakes of a vehicle, work done by the friction force between the brakes and the wheel reduces the kinetic energy of the vehicle and the temperature of the brakes increases.
The greater the speed of a vehicle the greater the braking force needed to stop the vehicle in a certain distance.
The greater the braking force the greater the deceleration of the vehicle. Large decelerations may lead to brakes overheating and/or loss of control.
Students should be able to:
• explain the dangers caused by large decelerations
• (HT only) estimate the forces involved in the deceleration of road vehicles in typical situations on a public road.

scopeNotes.statement: Poor condition of the vehicle is limited to the vehicle's brakes or tyres.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every item about the vehicle's own condition names only the brakes (worn pads, overheated discs) or the tyres (worn tread, poor inflation). Engine power, gearbox, suspension, steering and vehicle age are never taught as causes of a longer braking distance. Where such a factor appears as a distractor (q14) the rationale says explicitly that the specification limits poor vehicle condition to the brakes or the tyres.

scopeNotes.statement: Adverse road conditions include wet or icy conditions.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Adverse road conditions appear only as wet or icy road surfaces, and are always explained through the grip between tyre and road. No item asks for a coefficient of friction, compares named surfaces beyond wet, icy and dry, or treats fog or darkness as a cause of a longer braking distance - where fog and darkness appear (q14) the rationale states that they change when the hazard is seen, not the braking distance.

scopeNotes.statement: Estimating the forces involved in the deceleration of road vehicles is HT only.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Only q23 and q24 ask for a force to be estimated from a mass and a deceleration, and both are tagged tier 'higher'. Every foundation-accessible item on braking force is qualitative - a bigger force gives a bigger deceleration, a faster vehicle needs a bigger force to stop in the same distance - and none requires a value of F to be produced.

concepts.definition: The total distance a vehicle travels from the moment the driver sees a hazard to the moment the vehicle comes to rest: stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance.

The distance the vehicle travels during the driver's reaction time, before the brakes are applied. The vehicle is still moving at its full speed throughout, so thinking distance = speed x reaction time.
The distance the vehicle travels under the braking force, from the moment the brakes are applied to the moment the vehicle comes to rest.

concepts.term: Effect of speed on stopping distance
concepts.definition: For a given braking force, the greater the speed of the vehicle the greater the stopping distance. Thinking distance grows in proportion to speed; braking distance grows faster still, because the same force must remove kinetic energy that depends on speed squared.

A rough stopping distance for a vehicle at a typical road speed, found by adding an estimated thinking distance (speed x about 0.7 s) to an estimated braking distance. For a car, about 23 m at 13 m/s (30 mph) and about 96 m at 31 m/s (70 mph).

A graph of stopping distance against speed for a vehicle. The thinking distance contribution is a straight line through the origin; the braking distance contribution curves upwards, so the total line gets steeper as speed increases. A heavier vehicle sits above a lighter one at every speed.
The time between a driver seeing a hazard and beginning to act on it. Reaction times vary from person to person, with typical values ranging from 0.2 s to 0.9 s.
Tiredness, drugs and alcohol lengthen a driver's reaction time. Distractions, such as using a phone or a loud conversation, may also affect the driver's ability to react.

A simple method of measuring human reaction time: one student releases a ruler between another's open finger and thumb without warning, and the distance the ruler falls before it is caught is converted into a time. A shorter drop means a shorter reaction time.

A method in which a computer displays a signal at a random moment and records how long the user takes to click. It gives a time directly in seconds and removes the human error involved in judging and converting a ruler drop.

Reaction time varies from trial to trial, so several trials are made and a mean is taken, with any anomalous result identified and excluded from the mean. This makes a comparison between two students, or before and after a change, more reliable.
Wet or icy road conditions reduce the grip between the tyres and the road, so the braking force that can be applied without skidding is smaller and the braking distance is longer.
For this specification, poor condition of the vehicle means worn or faulty brakes, or worn or badly inflated tyres. Either one increases the braking distance.

Because stopping distance grows sharply with speed, and grows further in poor conditions, safe driving means lowering speed and leaving a larger gap when the road is wet or icy, and keeping brakes and tyres in good order.

concepts.term: Work done by the braking friction force
concepts.definition: When a force is applied to the brakes, work done by the friction force between the brakes and the wheel reduces the kinetic energy of the vehicle and the temperature of the brakes increases.

concepts.term: Braking force for a given distance
concepts.definition: The greater the speed of a vehicle the greater the braking force needed to stop the vehicle in a certain distance, because more kinetic energy has to be removed over the same distance.
The rate at which a vehicle's velocity decreases. The greater the braking force the greater the deceleration of the vehicle.
Large decelerations require very large braking forces. These may lead to the brakes overheating and/or loss of control of the vehicle, for example if the wheels lock and the vehicle skids.

For a road vehicle the braking force can be estimated from the mass and the deceleration using F = m a, after finding the deceleration from the change in velocity and the time taken. Emergency braking of a family car gives decelerations of a few m/s2 up to about 10 m/s2 and forces of the order of 10 000 N.

misconceptions.question: A driver brakes to avoid a hazard. What is the stopping distance?
misconceptions.correct: The thinking distance plus the braking distance.
misconceptions.misconception: Stopping distance is only the distance covered after the brakes are applied.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students picture stopping as beginning when the pedal is pressed, because that is the first moment something visibly happens to the car.
misconceptions.correction: The car is already moving towards the hazard during the driver's reaction time, and that thinking distance is part of the road used up.

misconceptions.question: A car's speed doubles. What happens to its braking distance?
misconceptions.correct: It becomes about four times as large.
misconceptions.misconception: Doubling the speed simply doubles the braking distance.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students apply the proportional reasoning that genuinely works for thinking distance to the braking distance as well.
misconceptions.correction: Kinetic energy depends on speed squared, so at twice the speed there is four times as much energy for the same braking force to remove.

misconceptions.question: A car's speed doubles but the driver's reaction time is unchanged. What happens to the thinking distance?
misconceptions.correct: It doubles, because thinking distance = speed x reaction time.
misconceptions.misconception: Thinking distance is fixed for a given driver, because it depends on how fast that person thinks.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The name suggests a property of the driver, and the reaction time really is fixed, so students transfer that fixedness to the distance.
misconceptions.correction: The reaction time is fixed, but the car covers more road during that same time when it is travelling faster.

misconceptions.question: What shape is a graph of total stopping distance against speed?
misconceptions.correct: A curve that gets steeper as the speed increases.
misconceptions.misconception: Stopping distance is directly proportional to speed, so the graph is a straight line through the origin.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Only the thinking distance contribution is a straight line, and students read that part as if it were the whole graph.
misconceptions.correction: Adding a curved braking distance term to a straight thinking distance term gives a total that curves upwards.

misconceptions.question: What is a typical human reaction time?
misconceptions.misconception: A typical reaction time is about two or three seconds.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Two seconds feels short in everyday life, and the two-second rule for following distance is misremembered as a reaction time.
misconceptions.correction: The specification gives typical values of 0.2 s to 0.9 s; even a full second of reaction time would be unusually slow.

misconceptions.question: Do all drivers have the same reaction time?
misconceptions.correct: No - reaction times vary from person to person.
misconceptions.misconception: Reaction time is a fixed human constant, the same for everybody.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Textbook questions usually quote a single value such as 0.7 s, which reads like a physical constant such as g.
misconceptions.correction: A quoted value is only a typical value. Real reaction times differ between people, and between trials for the same person.

misconceptions.question: Which factors lengthen a driver's reaction time?
misconceptions.correct: Tiredness, drugs and alcohol; distractions also affect the ability to react.
misconceptions.misconception: Wet or icy roads lengthen the driver's reaction time.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know bad weather makes stopping worse, and attach it to whichever part of the stopping distance they meet first.
misconceptions.correction: Road conditions act on the braking distance through grip. They do not change how quickly the driver's brain and muscles respond.

misconceptions.question: Worn brake pads are fitted to a car. Which part of the stopping distance increases?
misconceptions.misconception: Worn brakes or worn tyres make the thinking distance longer.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students sort every factor into one undifferentiated pile of things that make stopping worse, without asking which stage of the stop it acts on.
misconceptions.correction: Brakes and tyres do nothing until the pedal is pressed, so they can only affect the distance travelled under the braking force.

misconceptions.question: In a ruler drop test the ruler falls 20 cm before it is caught. What is the reaction time?
misconceptions.correct: About 0.2 s, found by converting the drop distance into a time.
misconceptions.misconception: The number of centimetres the ruler falls is itself the reaction time.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The quantity actually measured is a length, and students report it as though the instrument had given a time.
misconceptions.correction: The ruler falls under gravity, so the drop distance must be converted to a time using a conversion chart or s = 1/2 g t2.

misconceptions.question: A student's five ruler drop trials include one result far larger than the rest. How should the mean be found?
misconceptions.correct: Identify the anomaly, exclude it, and average the remaining trials.
misconceptions.misconception: Either every trial must be included in the mean, or a single best trial should be used on its own.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students are taught to repeat and average, but not to look at the values first, so anomalies are either kept or the whole set is abandoned for one favourite reading.
misconceptions.correction: Repeats are averaged, but a result that stands well clear of a tight cluster is an anomaly and should be left out of the mean.

misconceptions.question: Where does the kinetic energy of a braking car go?
misconceptions.correct: Work done by friction between the brakes and the wheel raises the temperature of the brakes.
misconceptions.misconception: The kinetic energy is destroyed by the brakes, or is stored inside the brakes ready for reuse.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The car visibly stops, so the energy appears to have gone, and the phrase the brakes take the energy is half remembered.
misconceptions.correction: Energy is not destroyed. The friction force does work and energy is transferred to the thermal store of the brakes, whose temperature rises.

misconceptions.question: Two identical cars stop in the same distance, one from 12 m/s and one from 24 m/s. Which needs the greater braking force?
misconceptions.misconception: The faster car needs a smaller force because it has more time and more road in which to slow down.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students confuse stopping within a fixed distance with stopping over a longer distance, where a gentler force genuinely is enough.
misconceptions.correction: The distance is fixed by the question. Four times as much kinetic energy must be removed over that same distance, so the force must be greater.

misconceptions.question: Why are very large decelerations dangerous?
misconceptions.correct: They need very large forces, which can overheat the brakes and cause loss of control.
misconceptions.misconception: A large deceleration is always the safest choice, because the vehicle stops in the shortest distance.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Stopping sooner sounds unambiguously good, and students do not consider what the force needed does to the vehicle.
misconceptions.correction: The force needed can lock the wheels and make the vehicle skid, and repeated heavy braking overheats the brakes so they work less well.

misconceptions.question: A 1200 kg car decelerates from 24 m/s to rest in 3.0 s. Estimate the braking force.
misconceptions.correct: About 9600 N, from a = 24 / 3.0 = 8.0 m/s2 and then F = m a.
misconceptions.misconception: Misapply F = ma when finding the force, for example multiplying the mass by the velocity (giving 28 800 N) or dividing the mass by the deceleration (giving 150 N).
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both a mass and a velocity are printed in the question, so students reach for the two numbers in front of them rather than working out a first.
misconceptions.correction: A force needs an acceleration. Find a = change in velocity / time taken first, then use F = m a.

misconceptions.question: Which parts of a vehicle count as poor vehicle condition in this specification?
misconceptions.correct: The vehicle's brakes or its tyres.
misconceptions.misconception: A worn engine, gearbox or suspension is what is meant by poor condition of the vehicle.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday speech a car in poor condition means the whole vehicle, so students name whichever part they happen to know about.
misconceptions.correction: The specification limits poor condition of the vehicle to the brakes or the tyres, the two parts that act to slow the vehicle.

misconceptions.question: A driver is holding a phone conversation while driving. What does this affect?
misconceptions.correct: It affects the ability to react, so the thinking distance is longer.
misconceptions.misconception: A distraction cannot matter so long as the driver is awake and has not been drinking.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn tiredness, drugs and alcohol as the named list, and treat distractions as a separate and much softer category.
misconceptions.correction: The specification says distractions may also affect a driver's ability to react. A distracted driver reacts later, or does not react at all.

misconceptions.question: On an icy road, why is the braking distance longer?
misconceptions.correct: There is less grip between the tyres and the road, so a smaller braking force can be used without skidding.
misconceptions.misconception: Ice makes the vehicle heavier, or stops the brakes themselves from working.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know ice is dangerous but locate the cause inside the vehicle rather than at the contact between tyre and road.
misconceptions.correction: The brakes still work normally. What changes is the friction available where the tyres meet the road surface.

misconceptions.question: A van slows from 18 m/s to 6 m/s in 4.0 s. What deceleration should be used to estimate the braking force?
misconceptions.correct: 3.0 m/s2, because the velocity changes by 12 m/s, not by 18 m/s.
misconceptions.misconception: Use the starting velocity as the change in velocity, even though the vehicle does not come to rest.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Almost every worked example ends with the vehicle at rest, so students learn the shortcut a = starting velocity / time and apply it without checking the final velocity.
misconceptions.correction: Acceleration is change in velocity / time. Subtract the final velocity from the initial one first; only when the vehicle stops is that the same as the starting velocity.

mcqs.stem: A driver sees a hazard, reacts, brakes, and brings the car safely to rest. Which distance is the stopping distance of the car?

options.text: The thinking distance added to the braking distance travelled
options.rationale: The specification defines stopping distance as the sum of the distance travelled during the driver's reaction time and the distance travelled under the braking force.

options.text: The distance travelled after the brake pedal is pressed
options.rationale: That is the braking distance on its own. It leaves out the road already covered while the driver was reacting to the hazard.

options.text: Only the distance travelled while the brakes act
options.rationale: The student equates stopping distance with the braking distance alone, ignoring thinking distance.

options.text: The distance covered during the driver's reaction time
options.rationale: That is the thinking distance on its own, which at normal road speeds is the smaller of the two parts.

mcqs.stem: A car's speed doubles from 10 m/s to 20 m/s. The driver's reaction time and the braking force are unchanged. What happens to the two parts of the stopping distance?

options.text: Both the thinking distance and the braking distance double
options.rationale: Only the thinking distance doubles. Braking distance depends on speed squared, so it becomes about four times larger.

options.text: Thinking distance doubles and braking distance quadruples
options.rationale: Thinking distance = speed x reaction time, so it doubles. The kinetic energy is four times larger and the same braking force must remove it over a distance, so the braking distance becomes about four times larger.

options.text: Thinking distance is unchanged, braking distance doubles
options.rationale: The reaction time is unchanged, but the car travels further during it because it is moving faster.

options.text: The stopping distance itself just doubles overall
options.rationale: Believing doubling speed simply doubles the distance, the student says stopping distance just doubles.

mcqs.stem: Two identical lorries brake with the same braking force, one from 15 m/s and one from 25 m/s. Which statement about their stopping distances is correct?

options.text: The 25 m/s lorry needs distance in proportion to speed
options.rationale: Treating braking distance as proportional to speed, the student scales it only linearly.

options.text: The lorry at 15 m/s needs a greater distance in which to stop
options.rationale: This reverses the relationship. For a given braking force, a greater speed always means a greater stopping distance.

options.text: The lorry at 25 m/s needs the greater stopping distance
options.rationale: For a given braking force, the greater the speed of the vehicle the greater the stopping distance. The faster lorry travels further while the driver reacts, and further again under braking.

options.text: Its braking distance is just under twice as long
options.rationale: Applying linear scaling, the student makes braking distance rise by the speed ratio (about 1.7 times).

mcqs.stem: What does the specification say about human reaction times?

options.text: They are the same for every driver, typically 0.7 s
options.rationale: 0.7 s is a commonly used typical value, but it is not a constant. Real reaction times vary from person to person.

options.text: They range from about 2 s to about 3 s for almost everyone
options.rationale: This is roughly ten times too long. Two seconds is the recommended following gap, not a reaction time.

options.text: They vary from person to person, typically 0.2 s to 0.9 s
options.rationale: The specification states that reaction times vary from person to person and that typical values range from 0.2 s to 0.9 s.

options.text: Every driver shares one fixed reaction time
options.rationale: Thinking reaction time is a fixed constant, the student gives one value for all drivers.

mcqs.stem: Five students measure their own reaction times and obtain 0.21 s, 0.34 s, 0.28 s, 0.52 s and 0.45 s. What is the best conclusion to draw?

options.text: Four of the results must be wrong, as only one can be right
options.rationale: There is no single true value for these results to be right about. Different people genuinely have different reaction times.

options.text: Everyone's reaction time is 0.36 s, the mean of the five
options.rationale: A mean across five different people describes the group, not any individual, and it hides the variation the data actually show.

options.text: The results are unusable because they do not agree
options.rationale: Disagreement between different people is the expected outcome here, not evidence of a failed experiment.

options.text: Reaction times differ between people, as expected
options.rationale: Every value lies inside the typical range of 0.2 s to 0.9 s, and the spread between them is exactly what the specification means by reaction times varying from person to person.

mcqs.stem: Which list contains only factors that the specification links to a driver's reaction time or ability to react?

options.text: Tiredness, alcohol, drugs, and distractions such as a phone
options.rationale: The specification names tiredness, drugs and alcohol as affecting reaction time, and adds that distractions may also affect a driver's ability to react.

options.text: Tiredness, alcohol, icy roads and worn brake pads
options.rationale: Icy roads and worn brakes lengthen the braking distance. Neither has any effect on how quickly the driver responds.

options.text: Alcohol, drugs, heavy rain and under-inflated tyres
options.rationale: Rain and tyre condition act at the contact between tyre and road during braking, not on the driver's reaction.

options.text: The driver's age, natural reflexes and their IQ
options.rationale: Treating reaction as an innate fixed trait, the student lists inborn qualities, not transient states.

mcqs.stem: A driver holds a long hands-free phone conversation while driving. What does the specification say about this?

options.text: It has no effect, as the driver's hands stay on the wheel
options.rationale: The specification is about the ability to react, not about where the hands are. It is the driver's attention that is divided.

options.text: Distractions may also affect a driver's ability to react
options.rationale: The specification states that distractions may also affect a driver's ability to react. A slower reaction means a longer thinking distance and so a longer stopping distance.

options.text: It lengthens the braking distance, not the thinking one
options.rationale: A distraction acts on the driver before the brakes are touched, so it is the thinking distance that grows.

options.text: It matters only if the driver is also tired or drunk
options.rationale: Distraction is listed as a factor in its own right, not as something that matters only alongside another factor.

mcqs.stem: In the ruler drop test one student holds a ruler above a partner's open hand, releases it without warning, and the partner catches it as quickly as they can. Which measurement is taken, and what is done with it?

options.text: The time in seconds is read directly from the ruler scale
options.rationale: A ruler measures length, not time. The scale printed on it is in centimetres or millimetres.

options.text: The number of centimetres is used as the time in seconds
options.rationale: A 20 cm drop would then mean a 20 s reaction, which is absurd. The length has to be converted into a time.

options.text: The drop distance is measured, then converted to a time
options.rationale: The distance the ruler falls before it is caught is measured, then converted into a reaction time using a conversion chart or s = 1/2 g t2. A shorter drop means a shorter reaction time.

options.text: The mass of the ruler is used to find the time of fall
options.rationale: The time of fall does not depend on mass. In free fall every object has the same acceleration.

mcqs.stem: A student's five ruler drop results convert to 0.18 s, 0.20 s, 0.19 s, 0.65 s and 0.21 s. How should the student's reaction time be reported?

options.text: Average all five of the results to get about 0.29 s
options.rationale: Including the anomaly drags the mean up by half as much again. Anomalies should be identified and excluded before averaging.

options.text: Take the shortest result, 0.18 s, as the best attempt
options.rationale: The fastest single catch is no more valid than the others, and choosing the best result biases the answer downwards.

options.text: Keep all readings, since none may be discarded
options.rationale: Believing every trial must be kept, the student refuses to discard the anomalous 0.65 s.

options.text: Discard 0.65 s and average the other four results
options.rationale: 0.65 s stands well clear of the tight cluster near 0.19 s and is almost certainly a lapse of attention rather than a genuine reaction. The mean of the remaining four is about 0.20 s.

mcqs.stem: At 20 m/s a rested driver has a thinking distance of 14 m, from a reaction time of 0.7 s. When tired, the same driver at the same speed has a thinking distance of 18 m. What does the data show?

options.text: The tired driver's reaction time has risen to about 0.9 s
options.rationale: Thinking distance = speed x reaction time, so 18 m divided by 20 m/s gives 0.9 s. Tiredness has lengthened this driver's reaction time by about 0.2 s.

options.text: The reaction time has risen to about 2.5 s when tired
options.rationale: Expecting reaction times of two to three seconds, the student reads the tired value as about 2.5 s.

options.text: The reaction time is unchanged; the car was faster
options.rationale: The speed is given as 20 m/s in both cases, so the extra 4 m must come from a longer reaction time.

options.text: The reaction time fell, as tiredness slows the car down
options.rationale: A shorter reaction time would give a shorter thinking distance, but the measured distance has increased.

mcqs.stem: Which pair of causes does the specification give for a longer braking distance?

options.text: A worn-out engine and an ageing gearbox in the car
options.rationale: The specification limits poor condition of the vehicle to the brakes or the tyres, so neither of these counts here.

options.text: Wet or icy roads, and worn brakes or worn tyres
options.rationale: Adverse road conditions are given as wet or icy conditions, and poor condition of the vehicle is limited to the vehicle's brakes or tyres.

options.text: Fog and darkness, which hide the hazard ahead
options.rationale: These change when the driver sees the hazard. They do not change the distance travelled under the braking force.

options.text: Driver tiredness and having drunk alcohol
options.rationale: Tiredness and alcohol lengthen the reaction time, so they act on the thinking distance instead.

mcqs.stem: A car is driven on an icy road at the same speed as it was on a dry road. Why is its braking distance longer on the ice?

options.text: The ice makes the vehicle heavier, so it takes far longer
options.rationale: Ice lying on the road does not change the mass of the car in any way that matters here.

options.text: The brakes themselves stop working when the road is icy
options.rationale: The braking system is unaffected. What changes is the friction between the tyres and the road surface.

options.text: There is less grip, so a smaller braking force can act
options.rationale: Ice reduces the friction available where the tyres meet the road, so the largest braking force that can be applied before the wheels lock is smaller and more distance is needed.

options.text: The driver's reaction time is longer on an icy road
options.rationale: Road conditions do not change how quickly the driver reacts; they change the braking distance.

mcqs.stem: A car has badly worn tyres. Which part of the stopping distance is increased, and why?

options.text: The thinking distance, because the driver is more cautious
options.rationale: Thinking distance depends only on the speed and the reaction time. How cautious the driver feels does not enter into it.

options.text: The thinking distance, because tyres are part of the car
options.rationale: The tyres play no part at all until the brakes are applied, so they cannot affect the reaction stage of the stop.

options.text: Neither, provided the driver brakes gently and early
options.rationale: Braking gently lengthens the stop further, and worn tyres reduce the grip available whenever the brakes are used.

options.text: The braking distance: the tyres grip the road less
options.rationale: Worn tread cannot clear water or bite into the road surface, so the friction force available for braking is smaller and the car travels further under braking.

mcqs.stem: Heavy rain begins during a motorway journey. Which action best reflects the physics of stopping distance, and why?

options.text: Slow down and leave a bigger gap, as braking needs more road
options.rationale: Wet conditions reduce grip and so lengthen the braking distance, while the thinking distance is unchanged. Driving more slowly and leaving a larger gap restores the safety margin.

options.text: Keep the same gap, since the reaction time is unchanged
options.rationale: The reaction time is indeed unchanged, but the braking distance has grown, so the total stopping distance is longer.

options.text: Brake as hard as possible each time, to stop sooner
options.rationale: Very hard braking on a wet road is likely to lock the wheels and cause a skid, which lengthens the stop.

options.text: Drive faster, to spend less time out in the rain
options.rationale: A greater speed increases both parts of the stopping distance, at the very moment when grip is already reduced.

mcqs.stem: On a dry road a car travelling at 31 m/s (about 70 mph) has a stopping distance of roughly 96 m, of which about 22 m is thinking distance. Estimate its stopping distance at the same speed on a wet road.

options.text: About 96 m, because the driver reacts just as quickly
options.rationale: The reaction time is unchanged, but the braking distance grows on a wet surface, so the total must be larger.

options.text: About 170 m, since the braking part roughly doubles
options.rationale: The thinking distance of about 22 m is unchanged, but the braking distance of about 74 m roughly doubles on a wet surface, taking the total to somewhere near 170 m.

options.text: About 48 m, as water lubricates the road well
options.rationale: Water reduces the grip, which lengthens the stop. It certainly does not halve the distance.

options.text: About 31 m, one metre for each metre per second
options.rationale: This treats stopping distance as directly proportional to speed. It has no physical basis and gives less than a third of the dry road value.

mcqs.stem: A force is applied to the brakes of a moving car. Which statement describes what happens to the energy?

options.text: Kinetic energy is destroyed by the friction in the brake pads
options.rationale: Energy cannot be destroyed. It is transferred out of the kinetic store of the car and into a thermal store.

options.text: Kinetic energy is stored in the brakes ready for later reuse
options.rationale: The brakes do not store the energy usefully. Their temperature rises and the energy is dissipated to the surroundings.

options.text: Friction does work, heating the brakes and slowing the car
options.rationale: Work done by the friction force between the brakes and the wheel reduces the kinetic energy of the vehicle, and the temperature of the brakes increases.

options.text: The kinetic energy simply disappears when the car stops
options.rationale: The student believes kinetic energy is destroyed, here simply vanishing as the car stops.

mcqs.stem: Two identical cars must each stop within the same distance, one from 12 m/s and the other from 24 m/s. Which needs the greater braking force, and why?

options.text: The car at 12 m/s, as a slow car is harder to stop
options.rationale: The slower car has less kinetic energy to remove over the same distance, so it needs a smaller braking force.

options.text: The car at 24 m/s needs less force, having more time
options.rationale: The stopping distance is fixed by the question, so the faster car does not get any extra road in which to slow down.

options.text: The 24 m/s car needs less force, with more road
options.rationale: The student thinks the faster car's greater road length lets a smaller force stop it.

options.text: The car at 24 m/s: more kinetic energy to remove
options.rationale: The greater the speed of a vehicle the greater the braking force needed to stop the vehicle in a certain distance. Four times as much kinetic energy must be removed over the same distance.

mcqs.stem: A driver brakes very hard to avoid a collision, producing a very large deceleration. Why is this dangerous?

options.text: A very large braking force is needed, risking loss of control
options.rationale: The greater the braking force the greater the deceleration, and large decelerations may lead to the brakes overheating and to loss of control, for example if the wheels lock and the car skids.

options.text: A large deceleration always means a longer stopping distance
options.rationale: A larger deceleration shortens the braking distance. The danger lies in the size of the force that is needed to produce it.

options.text: It is not dangerous, since stopping sooner is safer
options.rationale: Stopping in a shorter distance is useful, but the very large force required brings risks of its own.

options.text: The kinetic energy is destroyed at once, harming the car
options.rationale: Believing braking destroys kinetic energy, the student imagines that sudden destruction as the hazard.

mcqs.stem: A lorry driver brakes heavily and repeatedly on a long, steep hill. What is the most likely consequence, and why?

options.text: The brakes cool down, as the lorry is slowing
options.rationale: Slowing the lorry is precisely the process that heats the brakes, because friction is doing work on them.

options.text: The brakes overheat, so they become less effective
options.rationale: Work done by the friction force raises the temperature of the brakes. Repeated heavy braking gives them no chance to cool, and overheated brakes lose their effectiveness.

options.text: The kinetic energy of the lorry rises as it descends
options.rationale: The driver is braking in order to control the speed, so the kinetic energy is being reduced, not increased.

options.text: The kinetic energy is stored in the brakes
options.rationale: The student thinks braking stores the kinetic energy in the brakes rather than dissipating it as heat.

mcqs.stem: (HT only) A car of mass 1200 kg travelling at 24 m/s brakes in an emergency and comes to rest in 3.0 s. Estimate the braking force acting on the car.

options.text: 28 800 N, from the mass times the car's velocity
options.rationale: 1200 x 24 gives the momentum of the car in kg m/s, not a force. A force calculation needs an acceleration.

options.text: 3600 N, from mass x the 3.0 s stopping time
options.rationale: This treats the stopping time as if it were the deceleration. The deceleration is 24 / 3.0 = 8.0 m/s2.

options.text: 9600 N, from a = 8.0 m/s2 and then F = m a
options.rationale: Deceleration a = change in velocity / time = 24 / 3.0 = 8.0 m/s2. Then F = m a = 1200 x 8.0 = 9600 N, a typical order of magnitude for emergency braking of a family car.

options.text: 150 N, from mass divided by deceleration
options.rationale: Dividing 1200 by 8.0 inverts F = m a and gives a force far too small to stop a car in 3.0 s.

mcqs.stem: (HT only) A van of mass 2000 kg slows from 18 m/s to 6 m/s in 4.0 s while braking on a public road. Estimate the braking force acting on the van.

options.text: 9000 N, taking the change as the full 18 m/s
options.rationale: The van does not come to rest. Its velocity changes by only 12 m/s, not by 18 m/s, so the deceleration is 3.0 m/s2 and not 4.5 m/s2.

options.text: 36 000 N, from mass x the starting speed
options.rationale: 2000 x 18 gives a momentum in kg m/s rather than a force. A force calculation needs the acceleration.

options.text: 500 N, which is a gentle everyday braking force
options.rationale: This corresponds to a deceleration of only 0.25 m/s2, twelve times too small for the change described.

options.text: 6000 N, from a deceleration of 3.0 m/s2
options.rationale: The velocity changes by 12 m/s in 4.0 s, so a = 12 / 4.0 = 3.0 m/s2. Then F = m a = 2000 x 3.0 = 6000 N, a plausible value for firm braking on a public road.
